name: Zora Mitsui-Bankole
description: Zora Mitsui-Bankole is a Tier 3 performance artist and geneware enthusiast who became famous not for what she broadcasts but for what she refuses to broadcast — she shares only tactile sensation feeds, no visuals, no emotional data, no sound, just the precise physical sensation of existing in a genetically modified body that includes bioluminescent skin, a prehensile tail, and nerve endings calibrated for heightened texture sensitivity. Her feed launched in 2221 and immediately attracted a following among people who are touch-starved or physically isolated, particularly in the corponation quarter communities where overcrowding paradoxically produces profound physical loneliness.
cultural_impact: Zora's tactile-only format created an entirely new subcategory of neural-feed consumption and sparked a debate about whether sensation sharing without emotional context constitutes intimacy or its opposite. Her feed is prescribed by some Tier 2 therapists as a treatment for sensory deprivation disorders, creating an unusual crossover between celebrity culture and medical practice.
key_figures: Dr. Cassius Ferreira-Holm (the geneware sculptor who designed her modifications)
The Meridian BCI Ethics Collective (who both celebrate and scrutinize her work)
locations: Zora's studio, Tier 3 Arts Corridor near the old Wacker span
the Gray Zone's tactile art installation space The Nerve Garden
story_hooks: Zora begins feeling sensations in her feed that she isn't experiencing — someone has spliced into her tactile broadcast and is adding phantom inputs, slowly, subtly, to see if she notices before her subscribers do.

A Tier 5 pharmaceutical corponation approaches Zora to license her feed format for a new sensory therapy product, but the contract requires her to undergo additional geneware modifications she hasn't chosen — modifications that would make her feed more commercially 'optimized.'

A subscriber who has been using Zora's feed for chronic pain management dies, and their family claims the feed suppressed their ability to feel their own body's warning signals. Zora's feed is the only thing standing between her and a corponation-backed lawsuit that could set precedent banning tactile broadcasting.
controversy: In 2223, a journalist published an investigation claiming Zora's 'unmediated' tactile feeds are actually processed through a subtle emotional filter that makes physical sensations feel more pleasurable than they are — effectively making her feed mildly addictive. Zora released her raw BCI logs in response, but interpreting them requires expertise most of her subscribers don't have, and the debate remains unresolved.
